title: Visible gear on characters - what's actually worked for you?
author: SeasonedAdManager
selftext:
Solo vibe coder here, not a 3D artist. I've got Claude Code, Codex, Tripo, Meshy, Hi3D, Blender and MCPs up the wazoo, and I still can't nail this down. I'm not trying to one shot anything. When I find something that works well, I turn it into a skill and workflow. I use coordinators and sub-agents that are pretty well built out. New features can take a whole week to fine tune and implement before I'm happy. 

Across a few projects I keep running into the same thing. I want the gear you equip to actually show up on the character. Shirts, pants, hats, bags, armor, weapons, all of it, and I want it to look good while the character is moving.

What I've tried so far:

AI generated characters with Tripo and Meshy. They look great as a single model, but the outfit is baked into the mesh, so every outfit is a whole new character and nothing lines up between them.

A free base body with separate clothing meshes on top. Clothes folded inside out, skin poked through, and anything made for one body looked rough on another.

What's working best right now is one body built by a Blender script, with the outfit painted on as colour regions and things like hair, hats and bags as solid pieces attached to bones. Mixamo animations retarget onto it fine and nothing can clip. But it's basically recolours. I can't really do a hoodie vs a polo, or plate armor vs robes, without it looking off.

So I'm curious how other people are handling character design, animation and visible gear. Modular pieces on a shared skeleton, hand modeled kits, AI in the pipeline somewhere, or something I haven't thought of. How do you handle weapons and bigger stuff like armor? Any workflows, tools, packs or tutorials that made it click? Paid is fine if it actually works, and "you're overthinking it, just do X" is welcome too.

comments.author: loulo88
comments.body: What fixed this for us was splitting the base body into regions (torso, arms, legs, feet, head) and having each gear piece replace the body region under it instead of sitting on top. That way there's no skin to poke through, and a hoodie vs plate chest is just a different torso mesh skinned to the same skeleton. We do this on Forgebound, the medieval settlement game I'm working on, and the rule that saved the most pain was authoring every piece against one reference body and transferring weights from it in Blender (Data Transfer modifier) rather than trusting the AI mesh's own rig. Weapons and big stuff like shields or backpacks stay as rigid props on sockets.

replies.author: SeasonedAdManager
replies.body:
Create and animate your character/models in blender or wherever (tripo, meshy), ask it to make a video and then create a sprite sheets out of it. 

Or just make a 3d game and throw a pixel filter on it.

comments.author: Seven-Prime
comments.body: The one trick with base bodies is that you hide faces that are behind clothes. The collider is still there but skin never pokes through.
